unitTitle: Mental Health Support Systems and Crisis Response
title: Correction and reflection: advocating for accessible mental-health support in a community
focus: advocating for accessible mental-health support in a community
essentialQuestion: When self-management is not enough, what is the next step and who takes it with me?
keyPoints: Accessible mental-health support considers cost, language, disability access, transportation, wait time, culture, privacy, and crisis coverage—not only whether a service exists.
Match the response to the level of need: use a practical coping step for ordinary strain, add trusted support when functioning is disrupted, and use urgent help for immediate danger.

For advocating for accessible mental-health support in a community, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Write a peer-support response protocol: what to say, what not to promise, who to bring in, and how to hand off — then draft one short advocacy message for better support access.
studentTask: Complete a fictional support-plan card for advocating for accessible mental-health support in a community: identify one observable signal, choose one immediate coping or communication step, name a routine support route and an urgent route, and explain why the plan does not make a peer responsible for care.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in advocating for accessible mental-health support in a community; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the advocating for accessible mental-health support in a community task using the supplied fictional or public case.
